Homothety-dial survey: which proved laws slide into one another

Turning k with d = 0: three stops on the bare line, whole-number stops once the scale is pinned, and 20 of 65 law groups that slide.

Homothety-dial survey: which proved laws slide into one another (DRAFT)

DRAFT, Nov 26 2026. Part of Affine Composition Theory (repo: fused-hyperoperation-algebra). Asked for by Brennan: "I'd like similar surveys for the other dials as well", after the shape-dial survey, whose ask was "a survey of all of our laws that we've proven to see if the shape dial is able to move from one to another", then "check all laws ... to see if a new law emerges and what it might be for", with "a polishing step ... as long as it doesn't take too much effort from the computer". This page turns the homothety k (the circle operation a ∘ₖ b = a + b + k·ab) with the curvature dial d held at 0 and every other dial fixed. Checks: checks.py → checks_output.txt, 65 of 65 pass (numpy, scipy, sympy, mpmath; about 2 seconds), including 5 polish checks at 30 digits that cost 0.03 seconds in all. Law list: laws.py → laws.json. Pictures: figures.py → figures/. No Lean in this pass. Colour key: blue = our reading, orange = already known, grey = endpoints and background.

The result

First, the plain fact the whole survey rests on. Rescaling a ↦ λa sends k to k/λ (check A1), and a ↦ −a swaps k and −k (A2). So on the bare number line the k dial has only three stops: k < 0, k = 0, k > 0, and the two outer stops are mirror images. Every "slide along k" of a law on the bare line is a slide between those three stops; k = 0 is reached as a limit, because every coefficient is a polynomial in k. The sign itself only means something when the sign of the values does (chances, counts, sizes).

Second, the useful fact. k stops being a unit choice the moment something pins the scale: a top value 1 (chances, fuzzy measures), whole numbers (bits, copies, counts), a graph (an edge weight at fixed site weight), a fixed spectrum (a matrix), or a fixed curvature. Then k is a real dial and whole-number stops appear: −1/m, −q/(q − 1), −1, −2, q − 1, and the threshold k = 1 on graphs. On the negative side each stop is where the wall −1/k lands on a pinned value (m copies, the scrambled error (q − 1)/q, the top value 1, one half).

With d = 0, the 65 law groups of dial-catalog/ sort into:

  • 20 slide into another proved law, with the carrying formula exact along the whole dial.
  • 5 survive on part of the dial (Lee–Yang on graphs, holographic corner sums, Boolean logic, the prime gas, the logic/algebra group).
  • 2 are the dial itself (the core law; the proof that k is units). 2 are the odds dial t in disguise.
  • 0 plausible. 36 don't slide: they live on d, p, q or t, or k is only a unit there.

The leads, judged each on its own merits, in order:

  1. One-mode counts are the Katz–Panjer (a, b, 0) class (C2). The law with coefficients ∏_{j 0. That list is exactly the (a, b, 0) class (Katz 1965; Panjer 1981; Sundt and Jewell 1981 proved there is nothing else), with a = kz. The rule "k < 0 only at −1/m" is their termination rule, and it is the same arithmetic as Shirai–Takahashi's α = −1/m. Confirmed; known pieces. The one-line identification wasn't found stated. Worth one paragraph in dial-point-processes/ and repetition-dial/, because it gives those pages their standard name.
  2. Fused calculus slides from ordinary to product calculus (C5). D_k F = F′/(1 + kF) keeps the product rule and the fundamental theorem at every k: ordinary calculus at 0, Volterra's product integral and Grossman–Katz's geometric derivative at 1, and the hazard calculus of survival analysis at −1. The grain of a difference calculus is k (Hilger's time scales, Fisher's rule with a period, jets R[ε]/(ε² − kε)). Known; a clean organising slide.
  3. The alphabet ladder (C10). Error rates of q-letter symmetric channels compose by ∘ₖ with k = −q/(q − 1): bits and Haldane's map at −2, DNA (Jukes–Cantor) and qubit depolarizing at −4/3, erasure at −1. The cure model k = −1/π fills every gap. On values in [0, 1] the line splits at k = −1: chance "or" laws live at k ≤ −1, Sugeno measures at k > −1. Known pieces; the reading is ours. Useful as a map, not a theorem.
  4. Tunnelling is a k slide, not a d reading (C7). Averaged over the angle, the law of cosines composes by ∘ₖ with k = −2K: piling-up lemma (sphere), variances add (flat), mean resistance (hyperbolic). The background curvature enters through k; the law's own reading −Δ/4 = −k²/4 loses the sign. Known pieces, ours as one formula (from tunnelling/).
  5. Lee–Yang survives only for k ≥ 1 on graphs (C8). Here k is an edge weight and is not a unit. Known (Lee and Yang 1952).
  6. The prime gas keeps its continuation only at k = ±1 (C6). Known (Dahlquist 1952), as dial-survey/wall/ found.
  7. Tsallis–Rényi–Shannon (C3), Sugeno's belief and plausibility sides (C4), the counting stops (C9) and the corner expansion (C1) all slide and are all known.
  8. Holographic corner sums (C11) give the one new in-between number: the weighted sum of three regions' entropies is ≥ 0 for every quantum state exactly when k ≥ √6 − 3 ≈ −0.551 (proved in two lines, sharp at the perfect tensor). Not found in print, but it says little about geometry. A small sharp fact, not a lead.

New laws at in-between settings (section N). The in-between values that matter are the pinned-scale ladders above, and all but one are known. The one I found no print for is the holographic threshold √6 − 3 (N3). The three whole-number ladders form one orbit of an order-3 map k ↦ −1/(1 + k) (N5); I found no meaning behind that, so it stays a curiosity.

Figure 0. Top: on the bare line, rescaling moves k toward or away from 0 but never across it, and a ↦ −a swaps the sides, so the stops are k < 0, k = 0 and k > 0. Bottom: the stops that appear once a value is pinned. Orange is known; blue is the one new number (C11).

Figure 12. All 65 groups, sorted by verdict.

How I tested a slide

For each group I held d = 0 (and the shape, order, odds and ratio dials fixed) and turned k. A group slides when both ends are proved (a Lean module or a checked page) and the formula that carries one into the other is exact for every k. Because only three stops survive rescaling, "every k" here means: the formula is a polynomial or analytic in k, holds at k < 0, at k = 0 and at k > 0, and, where the scale is pinned, at every special value too. A move that only rescales another dial's weight is the t dial in disguise. Where k is only a unit (every k ≠ 0 is the same law), the verdict is no, with the reason.

C1. Corner expansion: inclusion–exclusion → sums → products — slides

Figure 1. Left: one fold of three chances along the dial. Right: ∘ₖ-powers of 0.3; repeated union at −1, repeated addition at 0, compounding at 1.

  • The formula. 1 + k(x₁ ∘ₖ … ∘ₖ xₙ) = ∏(1 + k·xᵢ), and the fold is the sum over the cube's corners with weight k^(|S|−1) (checks B1, B2; Lean circK_lift, Combinatorics.kfold_lift, one_add_foldCirc_eq_corners at k = 1).
  • Stops. k = −1: P(at least one) of independent events, the union rule (B3, circK_either). k = 0: the sum. k = 1: the product minus one. Powers: 1 − (1 − a)ⁿ, n·a, (1 + a)ⁿ − 1 (B4, wpow_lift, wpow_neg_one).
  • Matrices. With a matrix in place of a number the fold is det(I + kA), and the walls sit at k = −1/λ for each eigenvalue λ (B5; mathlib-map/ proves this is the quasispectrum). Here k is not a unit, because A is fixed.
  • Logistic and softmax. The normaliser 1 + (∏(1 + kxᵢ) − 1)/k runs from softmax with a "none" option (k → 0) to independent yes/no logits (k = 1) (B6).
  • Known: inclusion–exclusion, Sugeno's and Banon's Möbius masses, Fredholm determinants. Ours: reading the three as one fold. Verdict: slides; known.

C2. One-mode counts: binomial → Poisson → negative binomial — slides

Figure 2. Left: the chance of 0 to 6 copies in one mode at the same mean. Right: which k give real counts: every k ≥ 0, but only −1, −1/2, −1/3, … below 0.

  • The law. One mode with weight z has generating factor (1 − kz)^(−1/k), so P(e copies) ∝ zᵉ ∏_{j<e}(1 + jk)/e!. (Probability convention of dial-survey/ and DialSurvey.lean; repetition-dial/ uses the weight convention with the opposite sign, Conventions.weight_prob_flip.)
  • It is the (a, b, 0) class. p_e/p_{e−1} = a + b/e with a = kz, b = z(1 − k) (C1). Binomial at k = −1/m (C2), Poisson at 0 (C3), negative binomial with r = 1/k and success 1 − kz for k > 0, geometric at k = 1 (C4). The wall z < 1/k is the negative binomial's convergence condition.
  • k < 0 only at −1/m. The binomial row of the table has b/a = −(m + 1), and (1 − k)/k = −(m + 1) forces k = −1/m (C8). At k = −2/3 the x³ coefficient is −1/9 (C5). This is Katz's and Sundt–Jewell's termination rule, the same arithmetic as Shirai–Takahashi's existence rule for α-determinantal processes (α = −1/m), and Lean's kRise_fermi, kRise_parafermi, two_thirds_negative.
  • Physics. Mean copies z/(1 − kz) = 1/(e^x − k) with z = e^(−x): Fermi–Dirac at k = −1, Maxwell–Boltzmann at 0, Bose–Einstein at +1 (C6). Spread n(1 + kn) (C7). In the weight convention of repetition-dial/ the same formula reads 1/(e^x + k), with Fermi at +1. Lean: fermion_lift, boson_mode, boson_fermion_dual.
  • Known (orange): the (a, b, 0) class: Katz (1965), Panjer (1981), Sundt and Jewell (1981, the "only these three" theorem); α-determinantal processes: Shirai and Takahashi (2003); Fermi/Bose interpolation is textbook.
  • Ours (blue): saying that the dial's one-mode law is the (a, b, 0) class with a = kz, so the −1/m rule of point processes and of claim counts is one rule. I didn't find it stated in two searches (queries listed under Known vs new); it is a one-line observation, so it may be folklore.
  • Verdict: slides; the strongest confirmation in the survey, worth one paragraph on the two pages that use it.

C3. Tsallis → Shannon → Tsallis on the other side, with Rényi as the ruler — slides

Figure 3. Left: Tsallis and Rényi entropy of one distribution along k = 1 − q. Right: the excess over adding is exactly k·T(A)·T(B).

  • Tsallis' q-logarithm is the dial's logarithm with k = 1 − q (D1). For independent parts, T(A, B) = T(A) ∘ₖ T(B) (D2), and Rényi = log(1 + kT)/k adds (D3). At k = 0 both become Shannon (D4). Lean: tsallis_engine, renyi_additive, qlog_dual.
  • Known: Rényi (1961), Tsallis (1988), Sharma–Mittal (1975). Ours: nothing new beyond information-theory-full/.
  • Verdict: slides; known.

C4. Sugeno measures: plausibility → probability → belief — slides

Figure 4. Left: the normalisation μ(X) = 1 fixes k = λ from the point weights. Right: on values in [0, 1] the line splits at k = −1.

  • Sugeno's λ-measure, μ(A ∪ B) = μA ∘λ μB for disjoint sets, is the dial with k = λ. Normalisation pins k (E1): Σg < 1 gives λ > 0, where the Möbius masses λ^(|S|−1)∏g are all ≥ 0 (a belief function, E2); Σg > 1 gives −1 < λ < 0, where the masses change sign (the plausibility side, whose dual measure has weight −λ/(1 + λ) > 0, E3); Σg = 1 gives a probability (E4). Lean: lam_lift, lam_corners, lam_neg_one, no_norm_past_wall, dual_weight.
  • The split at −1. λ never reaches −1: the wall −1/λ must stay outside [0, 1]. The "or" laws of chances do the opposite: they need the wall inside [0, 1], at the cure share π = −1/k (where-k-moves/), so k ≤ −1. k = −1, the union rule, is the one value that is both.
  • Known: Sugeno (1974); Banon (1981) on belief and plausibility; the Sugeno–Weber t-conorm min(1, a + b + λab) (Sugeno; Weber 1983). Ours: the split picture. Verdict: slides; known.

C5. Calculus: ordinary → product calculus, with the grain as k — slides

Figure 5. Left: the same ordinary integral read through E_k(u) = (e^(ku) − 1)/k. Right: (1 + k)^(1/k) → e as the grain k shrinks.

  • Do the theorems hold for general k? Yes. With D_k F = F′/(1 + kF): the product rule D_k(F ∘ₖ G) = D_k F + D_k G (F1) and the fundamental theorem D_k(E_k(∫f)) = f (F2) hold at every k. The Lean module proves the discrete version at k = 1 (ftc, ftc_box, mint_lift) and the grain-h rules at every h (rate_product, ts_exp, ts_exp_mul); the rest follows by circK_scale.
  • Stops. k = 0: ordinary calculus. k = 1: 1 + (fused integral) = ∏(1 + f dx) = e^(∫f), Volterra's product integral (1887), and D₁F is the logarithmic derivative of 1 + F, the log of Grossman and Katz's geometric derivative (1972) (F3). k = −1: D₋₁F = F′/(1 − F) is the hazard rate, and F = 1 − e^(−∫h) (F4).
  • The grain. On a grid of step μ, (1 + μr)(1 + μi) = 1 + μ(r ∘_μ i) (F5): Hilger's time-scale calculus, and Fisher's rule for interest with a period of length μ. Shrinking the grain gives e (F6). The jet planes R[ε]/(ε² − kε) are the same slide: dual numbers (the derivative) at k = 0, two points a step k apart (the difference quotient) at k ≠ 0 (F7; Lean units_circK, ofTwoPt_twoPt, dual_units_add, split_point, dual_point).
  • Known: Volterra (1887); Grossman and Katz (1972); Hilger (1988), Bohner and Peterson (2001); Pap's g-calculus. Ours: nothing beyond calculus/. Verdict: slides; known, and the cleanest picture of what "turning k" means: changing the grain.

C6. The prime gas Z_k(s) — partly

Figure 6. Left: Z_k(2) along the dial. Right: the exponents of ζ(Ns) in Z_k(s); they stop after N = 2 only at k = ±1.

  • Z_k(s) = ∏_p (1 − k p^(−s))^(−1/k) = ∏_N ζ(Ns)^(M(k,N)/k), M the necklace counts, for every k (G1). k = −1 gives ζ(s)/ζ(2s), k = 1 gives ζ(s) (G2, polished in G5), k = 0 gives exp of the prime zeta function (G4). Every other k needs infinitely many factors (G3), and Re s = 0 is a natural boundary.
  • Known: Dahlquist (1952) for the boundary; Landau–Walfisz (1920) at k = 0; Julia and Spector (1990) for the primon gas. Here k is not a unit: the primes pin the scale. Verdict: partly (the product identity slides, the continuation survives only at the two stops); closed lead, as dial-survey/wall/ found.

C7. Tunnelling averages: piling-up → variances add → mean resistance — slides

Figure 7. Left: the averaged law sits at k = −2K. Right: the squared half-chord t; the sphere has a wall at t = 1/2, flat and hyperbolic space have none.

  • Average the law of cosines over the angle: the squared half-chord t = (1 − cos √K D)/(2K) composes by ∘ₖ with k = −2K, exactly, for every curvature (H1, polished in H4). Sphere (k = −2): bit flips and the piling-up lemma (H2). Flat (k = 0): variances add (H3). Hyperbolic (k = +2): barriers' mean resistance.
  • Is it a k slide or a d reading? A k slide. The law itself sits at d = 0 for every K; the background curvature enters through k. The law's own curvature reading −Δ/4 = −k²/4 is negative on both sides and loses the sign. And since rescaling lengths moves K and k together, only the sign of K (sphere, flat, hyperbolic) is invariant: the three stops again.
  • Known: each average in its own field (Anderson et al. 1980; Matsui 1993; Flory). Ours: k = −2K as one formula (tunnelling/). Verdict: slides.

C8. Lee–Yang on graphs — partly

Figure 8. Left: zeros of the dial gas on a ring of 10, scaled by k. Right: distance off the Lee–Yang circle against the edge weight k.

  • The dial gas Z = Σ_S z^|S| k^(edges inside S) (lee-yang/) has k as an edge weight, which no rescaling of z removes. For k > 1 (attraction) every zero lies on |z| = k^(−deg/2) (I1, ring and 3-cube; polished at k = 2 in I4); k = 1 is the free gas (1 + z)ⁿ. For k < 1 the zeros leave the circle (I2), and at the hard-core point k = 0 they sit on the negative real axis (I3).
  • Known: Lee and Yang (1952), via the lattice-gas ↔ ferromagnet map (coupling log k / 4 ≥ 0 iff k ≥ 1). Verdict: partly; nothing new.

C9. Counting with a pinned input: parity → OR → count → subsets — slides

Figure 9. Left: n trues folded at each whole k; the counting class at each stop. Right: the idempotent defect (k + 1)(k + 2).

  • [n]_q is n copies of 1 under ∘ₖ with k = q − 1 (J1; Lean qnum_eq_wpow). The input 1 pins the scale. Stops: k = −2 parity (⊕P), k = −1 OR (NP), k = 0 the count (#P), k = 1 the nonempty subsets (J2; fold_xor_trues, fold_or_trues, witness_fold). At whole k = q − 1 with q a prime power, Gaussian binomials count subspaces of F_qⁿ (J3).
  • Touchard polynomials T_n(k) give Bell numbers at 1 and the complementary Bell numbers at −1 (J4; dial_blocks_minus_one), and 1 + k(1 ∘ₖ 2 ∘ₖ … ∘ₖ m) = ∏(1 + jk), the rising product behind C2 (J5).
  • Bits stay bits only at k = −1 and k = −2: (a ∘ₖ b)² − (a ∘ₖ b) = (k + 1)(k + 2)ab on idempotents (J6; Lean idem_defect, bits_closed_iff). That is why the logic group and the Boolean-lattice group are "partly".
  • Known: Gauss; Tits (1957) on q → 1; Stone (1936); Uppuluri and Carpenter (1969); Wilf's conjecture that the complementary Bell numbers vanish only at n = 2 is still open (De Wannemacker, Laffey and Osburn 2007 settle most n). Verdict: slides; known.

C10. The alphabet ladder on [−2, −1] — slides

Figure 10. Left: the stops k = −q/(q − 1) and the cure-model band. Right: error rates of channels in a row pile up to the wall (q − 1)/q.

  • A q-letter symmetric channel that errs with chance e sends the letter to each wrong letter with chance e/(q − 1). Two in a row err with chance e₁ ∘ₖ e₂, k = −q/(q − 1) (K1; Lean qary_cascade with c = 1/(q − 1)). The wall (q − 1)/q is full scrambling, and it absorbs (K2).
  • Stops (K3, K4): q = 2, k = −2: Haldane's map, bit and phase flips, the piling-up lemma (haldane, bit_flip, piling_up). q = 4, k = −4/3: Jukes–Cantor for DNA and the depolarizing qubit channel (depolarizing). q → ∞, k = −1: erasure, amplitude damping, the union rule (amplitude_damping).
  • Between the stops, the cure model k = −1/π (where-k-moves/) gives a law at every k ≤ −1, with the wall at the share π.
  • Known: Jukes and Cantor (1969); symmetric channels; Haldane (1919). Ours: reading the alphabet size as a stop of k. Verdict: slides; a useful map, not a theorem.

C11. Holographic corner sums — partly

Figure 11. The corner sum S_A + S_B + S_C + k(S_AB + S_AC + S_BC) + k²S_ABC for three entropy vectors. MMI is the statement at k = −1; the perfect tensor sets the threshold k = √6 − 3.*

  • holographic-entropy-cube/ found that k = −1 is the only setting where the corner sum is ≤ 0 on every geometry (monogamy of mutual information), and that it is ≥ 0 for k ≥ −1/2.
  • Sharper: it is ≥ 0 for every k ≥ √6 − 3 ≈ −0.5505, and this is sharp. Proof: write s, P, T for the sums of single, pair and triple entropies. Subadditivity gives P ≤ 2s; Araki–Lieb on the purification gives 3T ≥ P − s. For −3 < k < 0 the sum is at least s + kP + k²(P − s)/3, which falls as P grows, so P = 2s is worst, leaving (s/3)(k² + 6k + 3) ≥ 0 exactly when k ≥ √6 − 3 (L6; if P ≤ s the sum is ≥ s(1 + k) > 0). The four-party perfect tensor, realised by a star graph (L1), meets it (L2). An LP over every vector obeying SA and SSA agrees (L3), and 60 random min-cut graphs obey both signs (L4). Polished in L5.
  • Verdict: partly. The new threshold holds for every quantum state, not just geometric ones, so it says nothing about geometry. A small sharp fact; not a lead.

N. New laws at in-between settings

I swept the dial between the stops in every group that slides. On the bare line nothing can happen between the stops, because rescaling carries any k to any other of the same sign. So every in-between law needs a pinned scale. What came out:

In-between setting Law Status
k = −1/m (between −1 and 0) at most m copies; binomial counts; α-determinantal processes exist Known (Katz 1965; Sundt–Jewell 1981; Shirai–Takahashi 2003). Proved in Lean (kRise_parafermi)
k = 2/m (between 0 and 2) permanental processes from m real Gaussian fields always exist Known (Shirai–Takahashi 2003); checked by simulation in dial-point-processes/
k = −q/(q − 1) (between −2 and −1) q-letter symmetric channels; Jukes–Cantor at −4/3 Known; proved in Lean (qary_cascade)
k = −1, −2 the only places where bits stay bits (OR, XOR) Known (Stone 1936); proved (idem_defect)
k = q − 1, q a prime power Gaussian binomials count subspaces of F_qⁿ Known (Gauss; Tits 1957); checked (J3)
k = 1 on graphs Lee–Yang threshold Known (Lee–Yang 1952); checked (I1–I3)
k = √6 − 3 corner sum of three regions' entropies turns sign-definite Proved here (two lines, L6); not found in my search
k = n(n + 1), −ℓ(ℓ + 1) the tunnelling page's rewind ladder From tunnelling/, not re-checked here
the three ladders one orbit of k ↦ −1/(1 + k) Checked algebra (N1); no meaning found

N1. The −1/m ladder

The rule that k < 0 is allowed only at −1/m is one fact seen four ways: claim counts (the (a, b, 0) class), point processes (α-determinantal existence), copies (Lean kRise_parafermi), and the coefficients ∏(1 + jk), which must stop before they turn negative (C5). Known; worth stating once in the repo under its standard name.

N2. The alphabet ladder

See C10. The alphabet size is a setting of k on [−2, −1], accumulating at −1. Known pieces.

N3. The holographic threshold √6 − 3

See C11. Proved; not found in print; small. What it might be for: a quick sanity test of entropy data from three regions (a negative value at some k ≥ −0.5505 means the numbers can't come from any quantum state). That is weaker than subadditivity itself, so the use is mostly as a sharp constant.

N4. What k = ±2 are

On the bare line ±2 are not special. They become special when a chance is pinned: k = −2 is the binary alphabet (wall at 1/2, XOR), and k = +2 is the hyperbolic average at unit curvature (no wall). The cluster of laws at k = 2 that lee-yang/ found (leverage, Euler cusp, rung 2) are not d = 0 laws or are unit choices, as that page said.

N5. One orbit of an order-3 map (curiosity)

Figure 13. k ↦ −1/(1 + k) has order 3 and sends copies −1/m to alphabet −m/(m − 1) to q-numbers m − 1 and back.

The map acts on the wall w = −1/k as w ↦ 1 − 1/w, the order-3 part of the cross-ratio symmetry. I looked for a map that carries one ladder's law to another's with its meaning attached and found none (N2: the copies law and the alphabet law disagree on the same inputs, and every k ≠ 0 is isomorphic to every other by scaling, so an isomorphism alone says nothing). Checked; not a lead unless such a map turns up.

The polishing step

Five checks are recomputed with mpmath at 30 digits: the negative-binomial series (C9), ζ(2)/ζ(4) = 15/π² (G5), the hyperbolic average (H4), the ring zeros at k = 2 (I4) and the threshold root (L5). Cost: 0.03 seconds in all. The rest of the checks are exact (sympy) or at machine precision.

Assumptions

  • d = 0 throughout; every other dial fixed. Laws that live at d ≠ 0 (relativity, the plane law, conics) are marked "no" here and belong to the curvature-dial survey.
  • "Only three stops" assumes the values can be rescaled freely. Where a value is pinned (a top 1, whole numbers, a graph, a spectrum, a curvature) k is a real parameter; each candidate says which pin it uses.
  • C2 uses the probability convention (Fermi at k = −1). The weight convention of repetition-dial/ flips the sign.
  • C5's continuous statements are symbolic (sympy) and numeric limits; the Lean module covers the discrete statements at k = 1 and the grain-h rules.
  • C6 is numeric at s = 2 for five values of k, with primes up to 2·10⁶; the boundary claim is Dahlquist's theorem as quoted by secondary sources (the original was behind a bot check for dial-survey/wall/).
  • C8 is checked on two small graphs; the general statement is Lee–Yang's theorem.
  • C11's threshold is proved for three regions only, from subadditivity and Araki–Lieb; the LP and random graphs are extra checks. Four or more regions were not done.
  • The verdicts are judgements grounded in the named Lean theorems and pages; no Lean was built in this pass.
